title: A Print on Her Skin
dek: A woman is found beaten beyond recognition near a downtown building. With no witnesses and no ID, investigators try something almost never attempted: lifting a fingerprint directly off human skin, using superglue fumes.
cardBlurb: A beating leaves a victim unidentifiable and a case with no witnesses — until an experimental superglue technique lifts a palm print straight off her skin.
source: Timeline built from a Forensic Files episode summary and transcript describing the August 1996 murder of Martha Hansen in Anchorage, Alaska, and the superglue-fuming, hair analysis, surveillance video, and DNA evidence that identified and convicted Evans Lee Curtis. Dates beyond the discovery of the body are approximate, drawn from the episode's own account rather than court records.

martha.name: Martha "Marty" Hansen
martha.role: 48-year-old mother of six, a regular at a downtown bar

curtis.name: Evans Lee Curtis
curtis.role: Acquaintance of Martha's daughter; met Martha weeks before the murder

gifford.name: Bill Gifford
gifford.role: Homicide investigator who pioneered lifting prints from skin with superglue fuming

events.title: A body found near a downtown building, unidentifiable
events.summary: Workers found a woman's body near a wooded area downtown. She had been beaten so severely in the face that visual identification was impossible, and her clothing was scattered across a 30-foot area.
events.detail: Investigators noted the extended nature of the assault — repeated blows to the head and upper chest, not a single strike — and the total absence of witnesses or a matching missing-persons report.

quote.text: It wasn't he just hit her in the face once. There were multiple blows to her head and her upper-chest area.

events.title: An unusual call: try to print the body itself
events.summary: Because the body hadn't been moved or exposed to rain or direct sun, Captain Bill Gifford decided to attempt something rarely tried — lifting latent fingerprints directly from human skin using superglue fuming, a technique normally reserved for glass and metal.
events.detail: The conditions had to be exact: no emergency personnel could have touched the body, the victim couldn't have been dead too long, and the temperature had to be neither too hot nor too cold for prints to survive at all.

events.title: A palm print, recovered against the odds
events.summary: Technicians built an airtight plastic tent around the body, raised the humidity with heated water, and used a heat gun to blow a deliberately massive amount of superglue fumes inside — far more than standard technique called for.
events.detail: On Martha's left thigh, the fumes revealed a fragment of a palm print, left by someone steadying themselves there during the attack. It was only the second time a latent print had ever been confirmed on human skin.

quote.text: We were ecstatic. This was the second latent print off of human skin that had been confirmed.

events.title: Unusual hair, snagged in the branches above
events.summary: Police found 35 head hairs tangled in low-hanging branches directly above the body — hair that didn't belong to Martha, apparently caught there during the struggle.
events.detail: Combined with the palm print, investigators now had two separate physical leads pointing toward whoever had attacked her.

events.title: Autopsy findings, and a very high blood alcohol level
events.summary: The medical examiner found a bite mark and signs of sexual assault, along with bloody boot impressions on her torso too indistinct to identify. Toxicology showed a blood alcohol level of .308 — nearly four times the legal limit.
events.detail: Investigators noted the extent of contact with the body suggested the attacker had spent real time with Martha, both before and after her death.

events.title: The hair points toward a distinctive suspect
events.summary: Analysis identified the branch hairs as Mongoloid in type — a category including Native Alaskan and other Asian-descent hair — unusually long at 18 to 20 inches, and chemically bleached unevenly enough to leave an orange tint.
events.detail: Investigators were now looking for a specific kind of person: a Native Alaskan man with waist-length black hair carrying an irregular orange tint from incomplete bleaching.

quote.text: This is one of the most distinctive hair samples that I've ever seen.

events.title: Bar surveillance tapes catch a clear image
events.summary: Police canvassed downtown bars for surveillance footage, since Martha's high blood alcohol level suggested she'd been drinking that night. One tape — made unusually clear by Alaska's near-midnight summer sun — showed a woman in a checked jacket walking arm in arm with a long-haired man.
events.detail: The footage came from a bar called the Avenue, which ran nine cameras covering nearly every inch of the premises.

events.title: The bar owner identifies the victim
events.summary: Bar owner John Pattee recognized the woman in the footage as Martha "Marty" Hansen, a regular customer who'd actually been denied service and asked to leave that same night for being too intoxicated.
events.detail: Martha had been missing two days before her children reported it, which was why police hadn't yet connected her to their unidentified victim.

quote.text: A tiny, little girl -- never caused a problem.
quote.cite: John Pattee, bar owner, on Martha Hansen

events.title: A tip from a concerned citizen
events.summary: When police published the surveillance image in the local paper, a woman called to say a friend had blurted out, a week after the murder, that he'd killed someone — miming either hitting or strangling his victim when asked how.
events.detail: She'd initially dismissed it as drunken bragging. The friend was Evans Lee Curtis, whose hair fell almost to his waist and who matched the surveillance image closely.

events.title: Curtis is identified — and denies everything
events.summary: Curtis, unemployed with no prior arrests, fit the surveillance photo closely. Police learned he'd left a pair of pants at another woman's home, similar to those seen in the footage — and testing found the pants spattered with blood.
events.detail: Interrogated, Curtis denied any involvement in Martha's murder and argued he wasn't the only long-haired man in Anchorage.

events.title: The hair matches, down to the uneven bleaching
events.summary: Curtis's hair carried the same distinctive, irregular orange chemical treatment found in the hairs recovered at the crime scene.
events.detail: It was an unusual enough pattern that the match was considered strong corroborating evidence on its own, even before the print and DNA results came back.

events.title: The palm print is a match
events.summary: Police took detailed impressions of Curtis's palms, focusing on the distinctive crease between his index and middle fingers that investigators had identified in the print on Martha's thigh. It matched exactly.
events.detail: The match left Curtis with a direct problem to explain: how his palm print ended up on a murdered woman's body.

quote.text: That presents him with a serious problem. How does he explain why his palm print is on a dead woman?

events.title: DNA backs up the print — twice
events.summary: Concerned the novel superglue-fuming print evidence might face legal challenge, investigators pursued DNA testing as well. Blood on Curtis's pants matched Martha's DNA, and so did a small pocket of blood found hidden in a worn crevice in the heel of his boot.
events.detail: The boot-heel detail corresponded to what looked like a heel impression on Martha's body, suggesting Curtis had stepped on her during the attack.

quote.text: In this case, it was forensically solid.

events.title: They weren't strangers after all
events.summary: Investigators learned Curtis knew Martha's daughter and had actually met Martha himself at a dinner party a few weeks before the murder, where she'd welcomed him into her home.
events.detail: Prosecutors believed the two recognized each other by chance after Martha left the bar, and that what began as a friendly walk turned violent when Curtis made a sexual advance she rejected.

quote.text: She had trusted Evans. She apparently had been an acquaintance with him.

events.title: A guilty plea, and 99 years
events.summary: Facing the combined weight of the palm print, hair analysis, surveillance footage, and DNA evidence, Evans Lee Curtis pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to 99 years in prison.
events.detail: Investigators described the case as a rare convergence of old-fashioned detective work, an experimental forensic technique, and luck — crediting the superglue-fuming print as evidence unlike anything used in an Alaska case before.

quote.text: I'm not aware of any other case in Alaska where a palm print, fingerprint, or any type of print has been lifted from a deceased person.
